identity.title: Lower-extremity edema: bilateral vs unilateral, pitting vs non-pitting (brawny), grade and level

technique.how: Press firmly with the thumb for at least 5 s over the dorsum of the foot, behind the medial malleolus and over the tibial shaft, then release. Note whether a pit persists (pitting), its depth and duration (grade 1-4), how high up the leg it extends, and whether it is symmetric. Non-pitting, firm (brawny) edema suggests lymphedema or chronic venous disease.
technique.prerequisites: Compare both legs at the same level; ask about duration, leg dependency, and new drugs (calcium-channel blockers, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs).
technique.contraindications: None; avoid pressing over cellulitis, ulcers or a suspected DVT.

interpretation.positive_finding: Bilateral pitting edema modestly raises the probability of heart failure in dyspneic patients but is nonspecific: venous insufficiency, drugs, hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis produce the same sign. Unilateral edema points to a local cause (DVT, venous obstruction, cellulitis); brawny non-pitting edema suggests lymphedema.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of edema does not exclude heart failure (pooled sensitivity ~50%); acute HF and HFpEF often present without edema.
interpretation.pitfalls: Dependent edema in chronically seated or elderly patients is common without HF; edema lags behind volume changes by days, so it tracks chronic rather than acute volume status.
interpretation.changes_what: Bilateral pitting edema plus elevated JVP should shift dyspnea toward HF and prompt BNP/echo; unilateral edema should trigger DVT evaluation instead.

estimates.target_condition: Heart failure (any) in patients with suspected heart failure
estimates.population: Individual patient data from 9 studies of adults with suspected heart failure (predominantly primary care / open-access referral cohorts)
estimates.reference_standard: Heart failure diagnosis by echocardiography-based criteria of each included study
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.53/(1-0.72) = 1.89; LR- = (1-0.53)/0.72 = 0.65; from abstract sensitivity 53% and specificity 72% (no CIs reported in abstract)
estimates.quote: oedema (72%) ... sensitivity of these features was low, ranging from 11% (added heart sounds) to 53% (oedema)

sources.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess. 2009;13(32):1-207.
Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med. 2018;25(1):3-11.
Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA. 2005;294(15):1944-1956.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on edema alone to diagnose or exclude HF, or to judge acute volume status in a hypotensive or oliguric patient.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Unilateral painful edema needs DVT evaluation; rapidly progressive bilateral edema with hypotension or rising creatinine suggests cardiorenal or cirrhotic decompensation and needs urgent assessment.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Grading of pitting depth and duration is subjective; presence/absence of edema is more reproducible than grade.

extraction_notes: Sens/spec entered as percent. The anchor RCE (Wang 2005, source 2) reports ED-specific LRs for peripheral edema in its evidence tables, but the JAMA full text is not accessible through PubMed/PMC (no PMC record) and the abstract does not mention edema, so no Wang estimate is entered. The ED meta-analysis (source 1) reports only ranges for peripheral edema in its abstract (sensitivity 0.29-0.77, specificity 0.67-0.89, 8 ED studies, HF prevalence 25-59%); the pooled point estimates are in its tables, which were not visible, so no estimate entry was made. Mant 2009 abstract values have no CIs; LRs were computed from the abstract sensitivity/specificity. No study separates pitting from non-pitting or grades of edema for HF diagnosis; the pitting/brawny/unilateral distinctions in the title are consensus-based pattern recognition, not quantified.
